And it is said
that he wrote two letters:
one to Marcian that he should kill [him],
and the other to Mundhir that he should go to Marcian and hear from him a secret word which could not be written in a letter.
The notary, however, when he had written the two at the same time and sealed them,
as if by mistake, wrote 'Mundhir' on the one for Marcian,
and 'Marcian' on the one for Mundhir.
And thus that letter fell into the hands of Mundhir,
and he was filled with wrath.
And he made peace with the Tayyaye {nomad Arabs} of Qabus,
and they invaded Roman territory together, taking captives and burning as far as Antioch.
Now King Justin thought that Marcian had informed Mundhir,
and because of this he was angry with him and arrested him.
Then King Justin, when his mind returned to him
and he saw that the disease of strangury had grown severe upon him,
summoned Tiberius Caesar,
and spoke with him many wondrous words in the manner of admonition and warnings, saying:
'Consider what you were and what you have become.
Honor your mother, who was once your mistress.
And also all those who stand here are your children;
and care for the soldiers.
And do not delight in blood,
and do not repay evil for evil.
Let not the apparel and the proud form of kingship deceive you,
as it deceived me also.
And behold, while I am yet alive, I am being stripped.'
These things and many like them [he said].
Then Tiberius fell on his face, weeping and tearing his hair.
And he commanded, and they raised him up,
and he with his own hands clothed him and crowned him with the diadem.
And he lived nine days after these things,
and he died in that great distress of strangury,
so that from his pain he wailed and adjured those standing by,
'Bring a sword and kill me!' {OCR?} ... Tiberius, three years.
Until this time,
all the kings were Romans, that is to say, Latins/Franks;
